stories.headline: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat after a week-long count
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's U.S. Senate race, which was called Wednesday after more than a week of ballot counting. He will be the first Black senator elected from Mississippi since the Reconstruction era. One Senate race, in Alaska, has still not been called.
stories.why_it_matters: The result enlarges the Democratic majority that takes over the Senate in January, which affects what legislation, nominees and investigations can move in the next two years.
stories.background: Mississippi held its Senate election on Nov. 3 along with the rest of the midterms, in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. The race between Colom, a prosecutor, and Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, was separated by a few dozen votes in early unofficial counts, and outstanding mail-in and affidavit ballots took days to tally. Mississippi is a reliably Republican state in federal elections; the BBC noted that President Trump carried it by 22 points two years ago. The state's only previous Black senators, Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce, served in the 1870s and early 1880s.

facts.text: Colom defeated Hyde-Smith in a race that was called on Wednesday, Nov. 11, after a prolonged ballot count.
He will be the first Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since the post-Civil War Reconstruction period, and the third in the state's history after Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce.
Early unofficial counts on Nov. 4 showed Colom ahead by 43 votes, 462,821 to 462,778, with thousands of affidavit and mail-in ballots still to be counted, according to local reports at the time.
Hyde-Smith's campaign said on Nov. 4 that it was confident she would be re-elected once every legally cast vote was counted.
The New York Sun reported that the win gives Democrats at least 55 Senate seats in the next Congress.
Trump won Mississippi by 22 points two years ago, the BBC reported.
Colom held his victory event at Tougaloo College, where The Guardian reported about a thousand people gathered.

Alaska's Senate race between Democrat Mary Peltola and Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan has not been called; a state judge on Wednesday denied the Peltola campaign's request for data on rejected absentee ballots.

stories.headline: White House tells Democrats their planned investigations could be criminal
stories.summary: White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter Wednesday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the Democrat set to chair the House Oversight Committee, saying Democrats' promised investigations of the Trump administration "may cross the line into blatant criminality." Garcia responded that the Constitution gives Congress latitude to investigate and said the president appears to have "something to hide." Democrats take control of Congress in January.
stories.why_it_matters: Congressional oversight is one of the main ways the public learns how the government is spending money and using its power; a fight over whether lawmakers can be investigated for conducting it would shape how much of that happens in the next two years.
stories.background: Democrats won control of the House and Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms and will gain subpoena power when the new Congress is seated in January. Garcia, a California Democrat who is currently the Oversight Committee's ranking member, posted "lawyer up" on election night and has said he plans inquiries into administration officials. Days before the letter, Axios reported that Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche did not rule out prosecuting Democrats over what the administration called oversight threats. The Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause generally shields lawmakers from prosecution for legislative acts.

facts.text: Scharf, the White House's top lawyer, sent the letter to Garcia on Wednesday; it says Democrats' pledges to investigate the administration "may cross the line into blatant criminality."
CBS News reported that Scharf warned congressional subpoenas could lead to investigations by the executive branch.
Garcia said the Constitution grants Congress "latitude to conduct investigations."
Garcia said it appears Trump has "something to hide," The Guardian reported.
The New York Times reported it was not clear what legal basis could support the threat, noting that the Constitution grants lawmakers immunity for legislative acts.
Garcia posted "LAWYER UP" on X on election night, and Axios reported on Nov. 8 that Blanche singled out that remark and would not rule out prosecutions.
Rep. Ro Khanna told Fox News that Democrats can pursue investigations and an affordability agenda at the same time.

stories.headline: House sets aside Hegseth impeachment articles 211-204 as 11 Democrats miss the vote
stories.summary: House Republicans voted 211-204 on Tuesday to sideline eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth brought by Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican. Eleven Democrats were absent, and several have since apologized as colleagues criticized them. Democrats say they will return to the issue when they hold the majority in January.
stories.why_it_matters: The vote was a formal attempt to remove the official running the military during the Iran conflict, and the seven-vote margin was smaller than the number of Democrats who were absent.
stories.background: Hegseth leads the Pentagon and has been a central figure in the administration's military operations, including the conflict with Iran. Massie, a Republican who frequently breaks with President Trump and is leaving Congress, filed the impeachment resolution on Nov. 9 and forced a floor vote without his leadership's backing. Republicans still control the House until January, so the measure needed some Republican votes and full Democratic attendance to advance. Impeachment by the House would have sent the charges to the Senate for a trial.

facts.text: The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday on a Republican motion that blocked Massie's impeachment effort.
Eleven Democrats missed the vote, and the effort failed by seven votes.
The resolution contained eight articles of impeachment, which Republicans sent back to committee, The Hill reported.
Massie filed the resolution on Monday, Nov. 9.
Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., one of the absent members, said rush-hour traffic caused her to miss the vote, the New York Post reported.
Absent Democrats apologized, The Washington Post reported.
Massie said he would force more votes that are difficult for Republicans in his remaining weeks in office, according to The New York Times.
Rep.-elect Zach Dembo, D-Ky., a former Navy lawyer, said it would be "premature" to discuss impeaching Hegseth.

stories.headline: Treasury Secretary Bessent moves to a military base after reported Iranian threats
stories.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved from his Washington-area home to a U.S. military base because of concerns for his safety, according to the Associated Press, The Hill and CBS News, each citing sources or officials. Several outlets attributed the move to threats linked to Iran. He joins other senior administration officials who live on bases for security reasons.
stories.why_it_matters: A threat serious enough to relocate the official who runs U.S. sanctions and the Treasury is a sign of how the conflict with Iran is reaching officials at home.
stories.background: Bessent has led the administration's campaign of sanctions and financial pressure against Iran, with which the United States has been in a military conflict. Cabinet secretaries normally live in private homes with a security detail. During this administration several senior officials have instead moved into housing on military installations in the Washington area, citing safety concerns. The reporting on Bessent's move rests on unnamed sources and officials; the digest summaries do not include an on-the-record Treasury statement.

facts.text: Bessent has moved from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a U.S. military base over safety concerns.
A source told The Hill the move was due to Iranian threats; CBS News cited officials describing Iranian threats to his life.
Recent U.S. intelligence showed Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel in the Middle East and elsewhere, according to the AP report carried by PBS.
Bessent has led the administration's economic pressure campaign against Tehran, The Wall Street Journal noted.
He is one of several Trump administration officials living on military bases because of safety concerns.

stories.headline: House Republicans pick Jim Jordan to lead them in the minority
stories.summary: House Republicans chose Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as minority leader for the next Congress, passing over Majority Leader Steve Scalise. Jordan said he will press the party's agenda in the remaining weeks of Republican control. On the Democratic side, Sen. Bernie Sanders said he will not back Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.
stories.why_it_matters: The leaders each party picks now will set how much confrontation or deal-making voters see from Congress over the next two years.
stories.background: Republicans lost their House majority in the Nov. 3 midterms, and Speaker Mike Johnson said he would not seek the minority leader post. Jordan, 62, chairs the Judiciary Committee and co-founded the hard-line House Freedom Caucus, which for years pushed against the party's own leaders. Scalise of Louisiana is the current House majority leader. Democrats are holding their own leadership debates, with some senators calling for a new generation to replace Schumer.

facts.text: House Republicans elected Jordan as minority leader for the next Congress over Scalise.
Scalise declined to commit to serving a full term in the next Congress, Fox News reported.
Jordan said Republicans would push their agenda in the lame-duck session while they still hold the majority, the New York Post reported.
Jordan, 62, is a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, and Politico reported his win raises questions about the group's future role.
Johnson announced after the election that he would not seek the minority leader job, and Scalise and Jordan both planned to run.
Sanders said he will not support Schumer for Senate Democratic leader; Fox News reported Sen. Elissa Slotkin took the same position.
The Hill reported that Schumer is telling colleagues privately he has the votes to become majority leader.

stories.headline: Petition forces a new House vote on Epstein files bill
stories.summary: A discharge petition led by Rep. Thomas Massie reached the 218 signatures needed on Wednesday to force a House vote on a second Epstein files bill. The legislation would let states sue the Justice Department over records it has not released. The petition bypasses House Republican leaders, who had not scheduled a vote.
stories.why_it_matters: The vote will test whether Congress can compel fuller release of government records about Jeffrey Epstein, a subject on which voters in both parties have pressed for disclosure.
stories.background: Jeffrey Epstein was a financier charged with sex trafficking who died in federal custody in 2019. Congress passed a law last year requiring the Justice Department to release its files on him, and sponsors of the new bill say the department is still withholding material. Massie, a Kentucky Republican, and Rep. Ro Khanna, a California Democrat, began a petition over the summer for a follow-up bill, the Epstein Files Transparency Act II. A discharge petition lets a majority of House members force a floor vote without the speaker's approval.

facts.text: The petition reached 218 signatures on Wednesday, one day after the House set aside Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.
The bill would allow states to sue the Justice Department, Politico reported.
Massie launched the petition over the summer to get around House leadership.
In September the petition stood at 216 signatures, and sponsors said the remaining ones would come in November, according to reporting at the time.
Once a petition succeeds, the speaker must schedule a vote within seven legislative days, according to earlier reporting on the petition.

framing.note: Casts it as a showdown driven by Massie, an "outgoing Trump foe."

stories.headline: Tomb of the Unknown Soldier guard calls for silence as Hegseth's group leaves Veterans Day event
stories.summary: A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier called out for "silence and respect" after laughter was heard from a group that included Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following Wednesday's Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery. A Pentagon spokesman said the sentinel had reminded everyone to maintain decorum. President Trump laid a wreath at the tomb earlier in the ceremony.
stories.why_it_matters: The moment drew wide attention because it involved the head of the military at one of the country's most solemn memorials, on the day set aside to honor veterans.
stories.background: The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery holds the remains of unidentified U.S. service members and is guarded around the clock by Army sentinels. Visitors are expected to stay quiet there, and the sentinel's words were a call for silence and respect. Hegseth attended the annual Veterans Day ceremony with President Trump, who gave a speech defending the war with Iran. The exchange was captured on video and widely shared.

facts.text: After the ceremony, as a group with Hegseth finished taking photos near the tomb, laughter was heard and the sentinel announced that visitors must maintain "an atmosphere of silence and respect."
A Pentagon spokesman said the sentinel had "reminded everyone to maintain decorum," The New York Times reported; the BBC reported the Pentagon backed the guard.
Trump placed a wreath at the tomb and spoke at the ceremony, where he defended the Iran war.
